Words | Xuhao Du

Editors | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Editor’s note: What does it feel like to fall for someone? Apart from the corners of your mouth curling up a little, some will say: “It’s my heart skipping a beat… uh-oh.” The heartbeat you normally never notice suddenly starts thumping when you meet someone you like. Changes in the sound of your heartbeat can tell whether you are falling for someone; more importantly, monitoring and analyzing that sound can help us check whether our hearts are healthy, which makes it an important guide in medical diagnosis.

Much the same goes for other organs, such as the gut. Put your ear to someone’s belly and, among all the noises you hear, besides the intestines crying out with hunger there may also be groans of pain: the gut is sick. Traditional tests for bowel disease tend to be slow and not very accurate, and worst of all, patients often go through misery and indignity (see the cover image; embarrassing, isn’t it?). Non-invasive acoustic diagnosis offers a promising way around these pain points.

If the healthy workings of the body were a symphony concert, the brain would be the conductor, front and center, and every other player would make its own sound under the conductor’s direction, together producing a harmonious, beautiful piece. This series introduces the notes each of these players produces, and the sounds they make when they play a wrong note. First on stage this time: the heart and the gut.

People often say humans are visual animals, but we are actually quite used to judging situations by sound. If your car’s engine suddenly gets much louder, for example, maybe the driver has been too busy driving to get it serviced, and it needs checking.

Or when you hear thunder rumbling, you know it’s time to go home and bring in the laundry. Sound can tell us a great deal. Unlike the eyes, which cover only a limited angle, the ears are a sensor with no blind spots, a full 720 degrees of coverage, as the Chinese expression has it. That is why, since ancient times, traditional Chinese medicine has treated listening as an important source of diagnostic information. And in 1816, Western medicine invented the stethoscope, which concentrates acoustic energy to amplify the sounds of the body’s organs, making them an important basis for diagnosis [1]. The organs most often diagnosed by sound are the heart and lungs, and the intestines. Today I’ll give you a quick tour of a few examples.

Let’s start with heart sounds. When you see someone you like, do you suddenly hear your own heartbeat? And when you think of a heartbeat, do you picture it like this?

In fact, the kind of trace we usually see is an electrocardiogram (ECG): the changes in electrical activity produced by each heartbeat. It sounds like “beep… beep… beep.” What you actually hear as your heartbeat, recorded as a phonocardiogram (PCG), really looks like this [2].

This is the waveform of the heartbeat you actually hear. A single cardiac cycle in fact produces several sounds, known as the first, second, third and fourth heart sounds. The first heart sound arises from ventricular contraction and the second from ventricular relaxation; the third is produced by the ventricular walls vibrating during rapid ventricular filling, and the fourth by the ventricular walls vibrating as the ventricles contract and blood rushes out.

From these heart sounds alone, a doctor can make a preliminary diagnosis of many heart conditions: mitral regurgitation (a softer first heart sound) or mitral stenosis (a louder first heart sound), for example, a clear mismatch in the closing times of the mitral and tricuspid valves (a split first heart sound), or coronary heart disease (a markedly louder fourth heart sound).

Bowel sounds have also been getting more and more attention in recent years. When you think of bowel sounds, is this what comes to mind?

Bowel sounds are not just the rumbling of a hungry stomach. Put your ear to someone’s tummy (especially the lower right part) and you’ll hear that the intestines are making sounds all the time.

W. B. Cannon began studying bowel sounds systematically in 1905, including how to classify them and how the gut produces them [3]. Later work went on to classify bowel sounds and to process them as signals, but because bowel sounds are far more irregular than lung and heart sounds, there are few examples of their use in clinical diagnosis. The main criterion is how often bowel sounds occur: a low rate indicates poor gastric motility. After bowel surgery, bowel sounds are used to judge whether intestinal motility has recovered, and hence whether the patient can start eating. Some studies also show that the rate and intensity of bowel sounds can serve as an indicator for assessing the migrating motor complex (MMC). The MMC is the cyclical pattern of rest and contraction in the gut; when you hear your stomach growl, chances are you are in phase III of the MMC.

Recently, the team of Nobel laureate Professor Barry Marshall has also started working on bowel sounds. Starting from a mass–spring oscillator model, the team is trying to build a mathematical model of bowel sounds and use it to decompose recorded bowel sounds in order to characterize the structure and activity of the gut, with the aim of diagnosing bowel disorders such as irritable bowel syndrome through long-term analysis of bowel sounds. Below is the team’s mathematical model of bowel sounds [4].

Like heart sounds, bowel sounds come in different types. Here is one way of classifying them, shown in the figure below (waveforms and spectrograms): (a) single bursts, (b) multiple bursts, (c) continuous random noise, and (d) harmonic sounds. Between them they cover virtually every type of bowel sound that can be observed, and the bowel sound we heard at the start is essentially a harmonic sound.

Here is a 15-second recording. Can you tell which type each bowel sound belongs to?

If you’re curious about the sounds of the various organs, we can go through them one at a time: how each sound is produced, and what it actually sounds like! That’s it for today. Bye for now!

About the author: Xuhao Du holds a PhD in acoustics from the University of Western Australia and was a postdoctoral researcher in Barry Marshall’s lab. His research covers machinery noise control and medical acoustic analysis.

References

[2] Sato, Yoshimi, et al. "Third and fourth heart sounds and myocardial fibrosis in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy." Circulation journal 82.2 (2018): 509-516.

[3] Cannon, Walter Bradford. "Auscultation of the rhythmic sounds produced by the stomach and intestines." American Journal of Physiology-Legacy Content 14.4 (1905): 339-353.

[4] Du, Xuhao, et al. "A mathematical model of bowel sound generation." The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 144.6 (2018): EL485-EL491.
